Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 103, verses 1–3:

It is Meccan according to the majority (al-jumhur).

Qatada said: it is Medinan.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Asr was revealed in Mecca."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Abu Muzayna al-Darimi, who had companionship (with the Prophet): He said: "When two men from among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) met, they would not part until one of them recited Surat al-Asr to the other, and then one of them would greet the other with salam."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By time (al-'asr),﴾ He, glory be to Him, swears by al-'asr, which is al-dahr (time, the age), because of the lessons in it, in terms of the passing of night and day according to the measured cycles and the alternation of darkness and light. Indeed, in that there is a clear proof of the Maker, mighty and majestic, and of His oneness. It is said that the night is called 'asr and the day is called 'asr, and from this is the saying of Humayd ibn Thawr:

"Neither of the two 'asrs ended, a day and a night, when they sought to reach what they desired."

It is also said that the morning (al-ghadah) and the evening (al-'ashiyy) are called two 'asrs, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"I delay him through the two 'asrs until he wearies of me, and he accepts half the debt while his nose is still rubbed in the dust."

Qatada and al-Hasan said: what is meant by it in the verse is the evening (al-'ashiyy), which is the period between the decline of the sun and its setting, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Amr sets out with us, and he has shortened the 'asr; in the first journey lies the spoils and the reward."

It is also narrated from Qatada that it is the last hour of the hours of the day. Muqatil said: what is meant by it is the 'Asr prayer, which is the middle prayer (al-salat al-wusta) that Allah, glory be to Him, commanded us to guard. It is also said that it is an oath by the 'asr of the Prophet (ﷺ).

al-Zajjaj said: some of them said its meaning is "and by the Lord of the 'asr," but the first is preferable.

﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss.﴾ This is the answer to the oath.

Al-khusr and al-khusran mean deficiency and the loss of capital. The meaning is: every human being, in trades and endeavours and in spending their lives on the affairs of this world, is in deficiency and in error away from the truth until they die.

It is said that what is meant by "mankind" is the disbeliever. It is also said that it refers to a group of disbelievers, namely al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Asad. The first is preferable, due to the generality in the word "insan" and because of the indication of the exception.

al-Akhfash said: "in khusr" means "in destruction."

al-Farra' said: "punishment."

Ibn Zayd said: "in evil."

The majority read "wa-l-'asr" with the sād unvowelled (sukun).

They also read "khusr" with a ḍammah on the khā' and a sukun on the sīn.

Yahya ibn Salam read "wa-l-'asiri" with a kasrah on the sād.

al-A'raj, Talha, and 'Isa read "khusurin" with a ḍammah on the khā' and the sīn, and this reading is narrated from 'Asim.

﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ meaning: they combined belief in Allah with righteous action, so they are in gain, not in loss, because they worked for the Hereafter and the affairs of this world did not preoccupy them from it. The exception is connected (muttasil). For whoever says that what is meant by "mankind" is the disbeliever alone, the exception is disconnected (munqati'). Under this exception falls every believing man and woman. There is no basis for what is said, that what is meant is the Companions or some of them, for the wording is general and no one who is characterised by faith and righteous action is excluded from it. ﴿And they advised one another to the truth﴾ meaning: some of them enjoined others to the truth that must be upheld, which is belief in Allah and monotheism, upholding what Allah has legislated, and avoiding what He has forbidden.

Qatada said: "to the truth" means to the Qur'an. It is also said to monotheism. Taking it in its general sense is preferable. ﴿And they advised one another to patience﴾ meaning: patience in refraining from the disobedience of Allah, glory be to Him, and patience in performing His obligations.

Placing the mutual advice to patience alongside the mutual advice to truth is evidence of its great worth and lofty honour, and of the abundant reward of the patient in what patience is required for. ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 153]. Also, mutual advice to patience falls under mutual advice to truth, so singling it out for mention and specifying it by explicit text is among the greatest proofs indicating its superiority over the qualities of truth, its excess of honour over them, and the elevation of its rank above them.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words "by al-'asr," that he said: "al-dahr (time)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him that he said: "It is an hour of the hours of the day."

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him that he said: "It is the period before the sun sets in the evening."

al-Firyabi, Abu 'Ubayd in his Fada'il, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he used to recite: "Wa-l-'asr, wa-nawa'ib al-dahr (and the calamities of time), inna l-insana la-fi khusr, wa-innahu fihi ila akhir al-dahr (indeed mankind is in loss, and indeed he is in it until the end of time)."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to recite: "Wa-l-'asr" "Inna l-insana la-fi khusr, wa-innahu lafihi ila akhir al-dahr." End.
